title: Sentences of 25 words at most
statement: Cap every sentence a student must act on, from instructions and questions to hints and feedback, at about 25 words.
example: The readability data the rule cites put a 14-word sentence at about 90% understood and a 43-word sentence under 10%.
detail: The reading project adopted the cap from a request to check the course is age appropriate, citing research that tied sentence length to comprehension at that grade band (R² = .55). It covers instructions, question stems, hints, second hints, reveals and the reply to a wrong answer, with story prose and the taught sentence frames exempt. A validator enforces it on written content, and the live scoring route holds its own generated praise and feedback to the same ceiling, since no static validator can see a line that does not exist until a child answers. The same cap is the practical rule carried to the Grade 9 unit.
against: The 25-word figure was set for one grade band. A later run found counter-evidence (`grade3-reading/ui-audit-2026-09-08/feedback-reconciliation/invariants.dom.txt`). A later run found counter-evidence (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/rules/content-and-copy.md`).

**Rule.** Instructions, question stems, hints, second hints, reveals, the reply to a wrong answer, and the guide's own think-aloud commentary: 25 words a sentence, maximum.
**Story prose.** Literature at grades 4 to 6 runs longer than anything else a child reads. Editing a narrative sentence down to hit a number is exactly the Lexile-driven editing R-KC-6 forbids.
26-word sentence, on the known ceiling debt list. Splitting it is owed, and doing so retires the entry.
Two surfaces are deliberately exempt, and a blanket rule would break both.

The corpus was already in band when this was written, at a mean of 11.5 words a sentence and a median of 10. The problem was the tail, and specifically the tail on the surfaces above: a 47-word line of modelled thinking, a 39-word hunt instruction, a 34-word reply to a wrong answer. Twenty-three sentences were split. That is the shape of this rule's value, and the reason it is a ceiling on one class of sentence rather than a target for the average: an average that looks healthy hides the individual sentence a child is stuck on.
